abstract.p: Disaster risk reduction (DRR) in multi-hazard regions requires locally grounded governance arrangements that connect policy, institutions, community capacity, local wisdom, risk data, and sustainable development. This study examines how village-level risk governance can support sustainable local development through a contextual policy model for West Sumatra, Indonesia. The province faces earthquakes, tsunamis, floods, landslides, volcanic hazards, and extreme weather, alongside diverse local institutions, including Nagari, the Minangkabau village institution. The study used a qualitative policy research design. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions (FGDs), and document analysis involving disaster management agencies, local government actors, village authorities, customary and religious leaders, volunteers, and community representatives. The data were analysed using thematic coding supported by NVivo to identify recurring policy issues and synthesise model components. The findings identified weak local regulatory frameworks, limited institutional coordination, inadequate human resource capacity, insufficient risk documentation, fragmented financing, limited integration of science and technology, and weak incorporation of local wisdom into formal disaster policy. The proposed model comprises nine interconnected components: C1 local regulations and institutional arrangements; C2 DRR paradigms, human resource capacity, and disaster literacy; C3 infrastructure, information systems, and preparedness facilities; C4 risk documents and integration into village planning; C5 DRR financing; C6 community participation and multi-actor collaboration; C7 science, technology, and risk data integration; C8 local wisdom and village social capital; and C9 sustainable development and village resilience. Coding-reference counts indicate recurrence rather than causal importance or policy priority. Sustainability provides the model’s overall purpose through livelihood continuity, essential services, environmental protection, and inclusion, while C9 specifies development outcomes for evaluation. The study contributes a synthesis of disaster risk governance, sustainable local development, and local institutional legitimacy. Local wisdom is treated as a potential resource whose contribution depends on inclusive participation and accountability.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Disasters in the 21st century can no longer be understood solely as isolated natural events, but rather as the result of a complex interaction between hazards, vulnerabilities, capacities, governance, and development decisions (Flores Durán & Alcántara-Ayala, 2026; Pescaroli et al., 2024; Raju et al., 2022). This paradigm shift is crucial because disaster impacts are never solely determined by hazard intensity, but also by how states, local governments, communities, and local institutions manage the risks inherent in people’s living spaces (Rahman et al., 2026; Tennakoon et al., 2025; Yildiz et al., 2026). The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030 (UNDRR, 2015) emphasises that disaster risk reduction (DRR) must begin with an understanding of hazard characteristics, exposure, vulnerability, and capacity. It also positions risk governance as a policy priority integral to sustainable development (Nekoei-Moghadam et al., 2024). In other words, disasters are not merely temporary disruptions to development, but rather indicators that the development process itself is not fully risk-based (Chmutina et al., 2021; White et al., 2025).

This perspective is increasingly relevant for Indonesia, an archipelagic nation located in a tectonically active zone, with diverse terrain and multiple hazards, ranging from earthquakes and tsunamis to volcanic eruptions, floods, landslides, droughts, and extreme weather. As a country frequently affected by disasters, Indonesia therefore needs a disaster management system that reaches all levels, from national institutions to communities (Benazir et al., 2023; Lessy et al., 2024). Within the global architecture, the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030 emphasises four key priorities: understanding disaster risk, strengthening risk governance, investing in risk reduction for resilience, and enhancing preparedness, along with the build back better principle (Benouar & Benmokhtar, 2025). These four priorities demonstrate that disaster management effectiveness cannot be measured solely by the speed of emergency response, but also by how effectively risk reduction is incorporated into policies, spatial planning, public investment, and local community capacity (Farinós-Dasí et al., 2025; Wolbers & Kuipers, 2023).

For Indonesia, strengthening the disaster management system has involved significant institutional development since Law No. 24 of 2007 concerning Disaster Management. However, the development of the national legal framework has not automatically resulted in equitable capacity at the local level. This implementation question remains relevant to the policy agenda of the National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA). The 2025–2029 National Disaster Management Plan and NDMA Strategic Plan provide national planning frameworks for resilience, prevention, mitigation, preparedness, and institutional support (NDMA, 2025b; NDMA, 2025c). NDMA Regulation No. 7 of 2025 updates the framework for disaster-resilient villages and urban administrative communities (NDMA, 2025d). These instruments provide a normative setting for community resilience. The analytical question is how formal responsibilities become sustained capabilities at village level.

However, a fundamental challenge remains the gap between national policy design and local implementation capacity. Research on evidence use, policy advisory systems, and policy styles provides supporting perspectives for examining choices that connect public issues, institutions, actors, instruments, and outcomes (Blum & Pattyn, 2022; Hussain et al., 2024; Tosun & Howlett, 2022). In the context of disasters, policies are effective when they integrate regulations, funding, interagency coordination, participation mechanisms, knowledge systems, and evaluation instruments that enable continuous learning (Kapucu & Sadiq, 2016; Nemakonde & Van Niekerk, 2023). Therefore, disaster policy studies must examine both the availability of regulations and how they translate into local authority, organisational capacity, actor behaviour, and collective community action (Haque et al., 2025; Kenmegne et al., 2026; Wowk et al., 2023). Within the core risk governance framework, this directs attention to the relationships between actors, the distribution of authority, and the quality of coordination. It also directs attention to the system’s ability to prevent the emergence of new risks resulting from development decisions that do not account for disaster risk (Hilhorst et al., 2020; Morrison et al., 2023; Onifade, 2023).

From a disaster management perspective, the shift from disaster response to disaster risk management has long been a scholarly focus (Cederlöf, 2026; Valencia Londoño & Valencia Londoño, 2024; Wolbers & Kuipers, 2023). Contemporary disaster management is no longer understood as emergency response alone, but as a cycle encompassing mitigation, preparedness, response, recovery, rehabilitation, and reconstruction (Rumpa et al., 2023; Sim & He, 2024). However, recent literature also shows that this cycle is insufficient without linking it to governance capacity. The quality of disaster management therefore depends on the ability of governments and communities to develop risk data, coordinate roles, and ensure sustainable funding. It also depends on their ability to link disaster management plans with development plans and incorporate local knowledge into institutional practices (Lee, 2019; Shah et al., 2020). In this context, weaknesses at the local level often reflect not only a lack of resources but also weak institutional arrangements. These arrangements fail to clarify responsibilities, resources, procedures, and long-term goals (Colocci et al., 2025; Fallah et al., 2024; Newman et al., 2024). Studies of climate adaptation, policy implementation, and metagovernance in other sectors inform this interpretation; they do not establish the conditions of the sampled villages.

Disaster risk governance thus becomes a key concept bridging policy and disaster management. Risk governance emphasises that risk must be managed through a network of actors involving central and local governments, communities, customary institutions, the private sector, civil society organisations, and knowledge institutions (Bendito et al., 2026). Thus, disaster risk cannot be treated solely as a technical responsibility of disaster management agencies. It is also a matter of governance, cross-sectoral coordination, knowledge distribution, and the social legitimacy of public decisions (Wolbers & Kuipers, 2023; Yildiz & Görür, 2026). DRR must be mainstreamed into all policies and investments that shape the future of society, as risks are systemic and can spread from one sector to another (Mechler et al., 2025; Yildiz et al., 2026). In other words, when policies on spatial planning, infrastructure, agriculture, settlements, education, and social protection are not integrated with risk analysis, development can actually produce new vulnerabilities (Auer et al., 2025; Masterson et al., 2023).

This argument is particularly relevant for West Sumatra Province, which, geographically and geologically, has a high level of exposure to various hazards, particularly earthquakes, tsunamis, volcanic eruptions, floods, landslides, and flash floods. The provincial risk context is illustrated by the 2022 Indonesian Disaster Risk Index, which recorded a provincial score of 144.39 (NDMA, 2023). The same document also emphasises that the areas along the west coast of Sumatra Island have a relatively higher vulnerability than other areas in the province. This situation demonstrates that resilience policies in West Sumatra cannot be developed in a generic manner. They must reflect the multi-hazard context, the uneven spatial distribution of risk, and the need for governance instruments that reach coastal areas, volcanic foothills, and river basins. Such instruments must also reach vulnerable villages that often have limited formal capacity. The 2022 index is used as a historical contextual indicator, not as a current risk estimate or a measure of each sampled village.

The urgency of strengthening risk governance in West Sumatra is increasingly evident in light of recent disasters. The 2024 Indonesian Disaster Data Book reports that rain-triggered lahars and landslides in West Sumatra on May 11, 2024, impacted 26 sub-districts across six regencies/cities. During the emergency response phase, the NDMA recorded 61 deaths, 10 missing, 7,490 displaced, and 56 injured (NDMA, 2025a). Physical damage was also significant: hundreds of homes suffered severe, moderate, or minor damage, or were submerged, along with damage to public facilities and places of worship. This event demonstrates that vulnerability in West Sumatra has manifested in social, physical, and institutional losses.

At the same time, the event demonstrated the interconnectedness of geological hazards, heavy rainfall, volcanic sedimentation, watershed management, and the preparedness of communities near risk areas. From a sustainable development perspective, such disasters not only claim lives and damage infrastructure, but can also interrupt livelihoods, exacerbate poverty, disrupt access to education, weaken health services, and increase fiscal pressures. Cross-country research connects economic disasters with sustainability outcomes (Malešević-Perović & Ćorić, 2024; Malešević-Perović & Ćorić, 2025). DRR is therefore relevant to the Sustainable Development Goals: development that ignores risk can produce recurring damage and undermine socio-ecological resilience (Wen et al., 2023; Yildiz et al., 2026). Discussions of disasters in West Sumatra should consequently extend beyond the disaster management sector to the protection of economic activity, environmental functions, residential safety, and vulnerable groups under multi-hazard conditions.

This becomes even more important when linked to regional development priorities. The Regional Long-Term Development Plan for West Sumatra Province 2025–2045, enacted through Regional Regulation No. 4 of 2024, connects civic development, progress, and sustainability with religion and culture (West Sumatra Province Government, 2024). This formulation demonstrates that long-term regional development pursues not only economic progress but also sustainability grounded in local cultural identity and social values. Consequently, DRR policies in West Sumatra should ideally not be positioned as a separate sectoral agenda, but rather as a foundation for realising the region’s own vision. Advanced and sustainable development will be difficult to achieve if disaster risks remain high, recurring losses continue to occur, and local institutions lack the capacity to systematically manage risks (Kalonga et al., 2025; Malešević-Perović & Ćorić, 2024). Research on the disaster-resilient village policy model can therefore link disaster policies with the vision of culture-based regional development.

The 2024 yearbook of Statistics Indonesia (Central Bureau of Statistics) reports that the village structure in West Sumatra is extensive and diverse; for example, Pesisir Selatan had 182 village-level units, while the Mentawai Islands had 43 (Central Bureau of Statistics, 2024). This scale and distribution suggest that strengthening resilience is unlikely to be effective if it relies solely on instructions from the provincial or district/city level without an operational design at the lowest levels of government. Poverty is also relevant to social vulnerability in both urban and rural settings. Poor groups typically have more limited adaptive capacity, lower access to infrastructure, more vulnerable housing quality, and slower recovery capabilities after a disaster. Therefore, village-based DRR is not merely a technical agenda, but also an instrument of development equity that prioritises the first to be impacted and the last to recover.

At the local level, formal administration interacts with social, cultural, and political relationships. In this article, village is a general term for the local governance arena. Nagari refers specifically to the Minangkabau institution that combines administrative and customary relationships; it does not describe every local unit in West Sumatra, particularly in the Mentawai Islands and urban settings. Disaster-resilient village refers to the policy programme or intended resilience outcome, rather than a separate administrative category. Customary leadership networks, collective norms, deliberation, and mutual assistance can provide resources for DRR, but their legitimacy and inclusiveness need to be examined rather than assumed. The study identified weak village involvement, limited human resource capacity, inadequate risk documentation, constrained budgets, and limited scientific and technological support. It also identified a need to connect local knowledge with formal policy. These reported problems concern the institutional conditions for local action, rather than merely the presence or absence of disaster response activities.

The Nagari offers an opportunity to examine policy design within a culturally distinct local institution. Its customary relationships, leadership, deliberative practices, and shared values may connect formal responsibilities with collective action. From a governance perspective, these resources matter because public decisions depend partly on whether residents recognise the authority and procedures through which they are made. Local institutional legitimacy is understood here in this relational sense. Recognition by customary leaders alone does not establish acceptance across women, younger residents, people with disabilities, or households outside influential networks. Villages can therefore be examined as arenas for local policy formulation as well as implementation, without assuming identical cultural arrangements or legal powers across the six study areas.

Indonesia’s disaster-resilient village programme provides a national framework that must be interpreted within these different local settings. The update through NDMA Regulation No. 7 of 2025 makes the relationship between formal policy and locally organised resilience relevant to current policy design (NDMA, 2025d). The concern here is not whether a generic programme exists, but how authority, operational support, social legitimacy, and development planning can be connected in practice. This distinction allows the study to move from a description of implementation constraints toward a contextual policy model, while keeping proposed arrangements separate from demonstrated policy effects.

More specifically, this research draws significance from the gap between dominant disaster management approaches and the complex needs of local governance. Many disaster policies at the regional level still tend to emphasise emergency response, logistics, and physical assistance. However, repeated incidents in West Sumatra demonstrate the need to reduce risks before disasters occur. This requires hazard-based spatial management, early warning systems, stronger community capacity, cross-sectoral coordination, and protection of vulnerable groups. These measures need to be linked to village development, while local wisdom needs to be integrated with risk data. Villages will remain reactive if policies place excessive emphasis on response. Conversely, if policies shift their focus to risk reduction, villages can develop into key actors in building sustainable resilience.

Within the framework of sustainable development, the disaster-resilient village policy model is also crucial because it can serve as an instrument for re-establishing the relationship between safety, well-being, and environmental sustainability. Disasters in West Sumatra have not only damaged homes and roads, but also affected agriculture, local trade, population mobility, the environmental quality of rivers, and family social resilience. Therefore, resilience policies cannot be formulated solely as disaster instruments; they must be linked to village development, poverty reduction, ecosystem protection, stronger disaster education, and risk-sensitive spatial planning. This principle aligns with West Sumatra’s need to ensure that regional development, grounded in religion and culture, is also risk-aware and disaster-resilient.

The contribution of this research is a village-centred policy synthesis organised around three concepts: disaster risk governance, sustainable local development, and local institutional legitimacy. Public policy instruments explain how responsibilities and resources are arranged, while the disaster management cycle provides an operational perspective on mitigation, preparedness, response, and recovery. These supporting perspectives do not constitute separate competing theoretical frameworks. The research question is: How can village-level risk governance connect formal authority, operational capacity, and local institutional legitimacy to support sustainable local development under multi-hazard conditions? The present study focuses on how these governance concerns can be connected within the village decision-making arena and oriented toward development outcomes. Its novelty is this analytical integration, rather than a claim that disaster governance or local wisdom has not previously been studied in West Sumatra. Sustainable local development provides the purpose of the analysis; disaster risk governance explains the organisation of collective action; and local institutional legitimacy directs attention to authority, participation, and accountability. sec.title: 2.1. Institutional position and operational authority
sec.p: Over the past two decades, disaster studies have shifted from a strong focus on natural hazards to greater emphasis on risk, vulnerability, capacity, governance, and resilience. This shift is not simply a change in terminology, but rather an epistemological and policy shift. Earlier approaches treated disasters primarily as natural events requiring emergency responses. More recent approaches understand disasters as the result of interactions among hazards, exposure, vulnerability, capacity, and human development decisions (Wolbers et al., 2021; Yildiz et al., 2026). Therefore, DRR is no longer simply understood as a series of post-event actions, but as a long-term process to prevent the formation of new risks, reduce existing risks, and enhance the resilience of communities and institutions (Imperiale & Vanclay, 2021). The Sendai Framework 2015–2030 affirms this shift by prioritising disaster risk understanding, strengthening risk governance, investing in resilience, and strengthening preparedness as four key priorities for global action (UNDRR, 2015). Disaster studies are therefore increasingly connected to research on public policy, governance, development, and social change. Disaster risk is understood as a problem shaped by collective decisions and institutional design, which can also help reduce it (Reinhardt & Ross, 2019).

In this context, recent international literature demonstrates that the concept of disaster risk governance is a crucial element in understanding why some regions are better prepared for disasters than others, even when the types of hazards are relatively similar (Woodall et al., 2024). Studies of disaster reduction and changing vulnerability draw attention to fatalities, affected populations, and economic losses (Formetta & Feyen, 2019; Lunga et al., 2025). These outcomes do not isolate the effect of governance. They nevertheless shift analytical attention beyond infrastructure availability or the frequency of emergency response exercises. The focus extends to authority arrangements, coordination between actors, the division of roles, accountability mechanisms, and institutional learning from previous disasters. DRR therefore concerns both actions during a disaster and the organisation of government and society before it occurs. This perspective treats disaster management as a broader governmental concern that extends beyond technical responsibilities to include development planning, spatial planning, budgeting, education, social protection, and state-society relations (Nemakonde & Van Niekerk, 2023).

Indonesia’s policy context provides a normative basis for this institutional question. Law No. 24 of 2007 establishes the disaster management framework, while the 2025–2029 national disaster plan and NDMA strategic plan set planning directions (NDMA, 2025b; NDMA, 2025c). Regulation No. 7 of 2025 specifically concerns disaster-resilient villages and urban administrative communities (NDMA, 2025d). The existence of these instruments does not resolve how local units obtain authority, resources, and support. This study examines the local governance relationships needed to connect formal responsibilities with action, rather than assuming that national policy adoption demonstrates local capacity.

National policy development does not resolve the relationship between formal mandates and operational capacity at the grassroots level. In West Sumatra, Nagari institutions combine administrative responsibilities with customary relationships, while other local units operate through different cultural and administrative arrangements. The institutional issue is therefore more specific than a general shortage of community participation: it concerns how local units can exercise an authorised role, obtain technical and financial support, and influence decisions that affect exposure and vulnerability. The study examines this issue through reported constraints in regulation, coordination, capacity, and planning. It does not assume that every sampled locality possesses the same institutional structure.

sec.title: 2.2. Local knowledge and institutional legitimacy
sec.p: Recent literature also shows a growing focus on the concepts of community resilience and community-based DRR. However, the use of the term “community” in many studies is often too general. Many studies discuss community participation, community preparedness, or community resilience, but do not always examine social structures, local legitimacy, power dynamics, or the community’s relationship with formal institutions in detail (Luo et al., 2025). In many cases, communities are treated as homogeneous entities assumed to share common interests, capacities, and orientations. However, communities comprise diverse actors with varying levels of influence and operate within heterogeneous cultural and institutional contexts (Fuhse, 2023; Geissinger et al., 2026). Therefore, contemporary studies tend to emphasise the need for a resilience framework that is context-sensitive, adaptive to local actors, and able to interpret the interactions between social capacity, institutional capacity, and the policy environment. In this sense, community resilience cannot be separated from the quality of local governance in which the community operates (Lowe et al., 2024). The organisational literature is used here to question assumptions of community homogeneity, not as direct empirical evidence about disaster governance in the six sites.

Another important research trend is the growing emphasis on local knowledge, indigenous knowledge, and local wisdom in DRR. Recent literature shows that local knowledge is not merely a remnant of cultural traditions, but can serve as a crucial tool for interpreting environmental signals, understanding the history of hazards, building legitimacy for collective action, and mobilising rapid social responses (Hadlos et al., 2022). In many cases, local knowledge can provide a useful route for bridging technical understanding with everyday community practices. Studies of local knowledge and culturally situated hazard responses support examining how scientific and local knowledge can be connected in context (Hirono & Nurdin, 2024; Rahman et al., 2026). Related research on policy preferences and pro-environmental behaviour highlights the relevance of group identities and culture; these supporting perspectives do not demonstrate the effectiveness of disaster policy in the sampled villages (Siddiqi & Wolters, 2023; Tam, 2025).

The social relationships surrounding a Nagari may enable deliberation, mutual assistance, and locally meaningful communication. They also raise questions about whose knowledge is recognised, whose interests enter collective decisions, and how customary influence relates to public accountability. Cultural legitimacy cannot be inferred from the administrative label of a locality. Formal policy must therefore connect with local practices while preserving opportunities for disagreement, representation, and inclusion. This institutional perspective complements the literature on local knowledge by asking how that knowledge enters decisions, rather than treating its existence as sufficient evidence of resilience.

sec.title: 2.3. Risk governance and sustainable local development
sec.p: Another important research direction concerns the growing relationship between DRR and sustainable development. DRR is a prerequisite for achieving the 2030 Agenda, as development that does not account for risk will ultimately produce new vulnerabilities, increase losses, and erode development gains (Wen et al., 2023). Disasters can no longer be separated from issues of economic sustainability, the environment, infrastructure, and social welfare. When a region builds settlements, infrastructure, economic centres, or tourist areas in vulnerable areas without considering risks, development itself can generate risk. Conversely, when risk reduction is integrated into development planning, development becomes a means to improve safety, resilience, and sustainability (Thomalla et al., 2018; Wilkinson & Campbell, 2022). The research agenda articulated by Imperiale & Vanclay (2022) explicitly connects DRR, community resilience, and sustainable development. Their conceptual analysis (Imperiale & Vanclay, 2021) examines the social dimensions of risk and barriers to that connection. Here, the unresolved issue is how these broad relationships become operational in village plans, budget choices, and decisions about services, livelihoods, and environmental functions.

The literature supports three connected but unresolved questions. First, how can culturally distinct local governance units exercise an effective role within multilevel disaster governance? Second, how can local wisdom be incorporated into formal risk decisions without assuming that traditional authority is uniformly inclusive? Third, how can village disaster governance become part of routine development planning, budgeting, and evaluation? Existing research establishes the relevance of governance, community resilience, and local knowledge; this study examines their connection through a contextual policy design for West Sumatra.

These questions define the analytical gap rather than a predetermined list of model components. Institutional capacity and collaboration are examined as conditions connecting the three core concepts. The study used qualitative evidence to organise reported problems and translate them into proposed policy functions. For example, a gap in risk documentation raises a question about the relationship between risk knowledge and funded development decisions; it does not by itself validate a particular planning intervention. Likewise, a reference to mutual assistance identifies a potentially useful social practice, but does not establish equitable participation or effectiveness. This distinction between empirical themes and policy propositions guides the nine-component synthesis developed below. The expected contribution is an explicit account of the relationships among mandates, capabilities, knowledge, resources, and locally legitimate action in pursuit of sustainable development. Comparative testing is needed to assess whether those relationships operate as proposed in different village and hazard settings.

sec.title: 3. Method
sec.p: This study employed qualitative policy research to examine how disaster-resilient village policy can be contextualised in West Sumatra. Field activities were centered in six disaster-prone districts/cities representing various multi-disaster contexts over the period 2024–2025. Padang City and Pesisir Selatan represented coastal earthquake-tsunami and flood exposure, while Padang Pariaman and Agam represented earthquake, landslide, and hydrometeorological risks. Tanah Datar was included for its experience of volcanic hazards, rain-triggered lahars, and landslides, and the Mentawai Islands for their small-island earthquake-tsunami vulnerability. These sites were selected to capture variation in hazard exposure, administrative capacity and village institutional context. The site selection therefore followed a maximum-variation logic rather than a statistical sampling logic.

The study involved 36 informants selected through purposive sampling to include knowledge of policy responsibilities, implementation constraints, and community practices across governance levels. There were 22 informants who participated in the focus group discussions (FGDs), and 14 informants who participated in both the FGD and interviews. The informants were provincial and district/city disaster management officials, regional planning and village development officials, village heads and other village officials, customary leaders, religious leaders, disaster volunteers, community representatives, and academics or practitioners with expertise in public policy and disaster management. The sampling rationale was analytical coverage rather than statistical representativeness. Thematic sufficiency was judged through recurrence of issues concerning regulations, authority, risk documents, financing, capacity, local wisdom, and collaboration in the pooled material. This judgement should not be interpreted as evidence of saturation within every actor category or site. The aggregate sample size alone does not establish balanced coverage of the eight actor categories or the six study areas. Table 3 therefore reports actor categories and their sampling rationale without numerical allocations by category or study area.

Public policy and disaster management expertise

sec.p: Data collection used three complementary techniques: semi-structured interviews, FGDs, and document analysis. Twenty-four semi-structured interviews were conducted to obtain individual accounts of policy implementation, coordination problems, institutional capacity and local practices. Four FGDs were conducted to examine collective interpretations and interactions among actors. These comprised one provincial policy FGD, one district/city government FGD, one village-level FGD involving village authorities and volunteers, and one community and sociocultural FGD involving customary leaders, religious leaders, and community representatives. Each FGD involved approximately six to eight participants and lasted between 90 and 120 minutes. Interviews generally lasted between 45 and 75 minutes. Document analysis covered national and regional disaster management regulations, the Indonesian Disaster Risk Index, disaster data books, West Sumatra planning documents, local government reports, village planning documents where available, disaster management plans, contingency-related materials and relevant academic literature. Document analysis was used not only to contextualise interview data but also to compare formal policy expectations with the administrative realities reported by field actors.

Data analysis followed an interactive qualitative process supported by NVivo. Interview and FGDs recordings were transcribed and combined with field notes and documentary materials. Open coding identified meaning units concerning regulations, authority, capacity, infrastructure, risk documents, financing, participation, technology, local wisdom, and sustainability. Focused coding grouped related issues by the governance function they concerned. For example, local rules, authority, policy harmonisation, and coordination procedures were grouped under regulations and institutions. Risk assessments, disaster plans, contingency arrangements, and development-plan integration formed the risk documents and planning dimension. Matrix coding compared themes across actor categories and source types. Model synthesis then translated the thematic dimensions into proposed policy functions, informed by disaster risk governance, sustainable local development, and local institutional legitimacy. Public policy instruments and the disaster management cycle supported this interpretation. Credibility was supported by source and method triangulation, examination of analytical memos, and repeated reading of coded extracts and field materials. These procedures supported thematic interpretation; they did not constitute implementation testing or validation of the model’s causal relationships. Table 4 summarises the data sources and their analytical use.

sec.p: The nine dimensions were distinguished by their principal policy function. Preparedness facilities concern operational provision, whereas science and risk data concern the production and use of knowledge; participation concerns collective decision-making, whereas local wisdom concerns cultural and relational resources. Related themes can therefore be connected without merging them into an inconsistent component list. Each dimension was translated into a proposed response to a reported problem, as illustrated in Table 5. The first column paraphrases issues in the reported findings; it is not a set of verbatim quotations or a recovered chronological coding log. Table 5 was cross-checked against the original NVivo project, the relevant coded extracts, and the analytical memos. The check was used to confirm that the mapping from reported themes to the C1–C9 components remained consistent with the underlying qualitative analysis.
