sec.p: Coding-reference counts describe recurrence within the analysed corpus. They are not unique-participant counts, measures of agreement, standardised scores, or estimates of prevalence. Counts may be affected by source length, repeated references by one participant, group interaction, document coverage, and coding decisions. Frequency, perceived salience, analytical importance, and policy priority are therefore distinguished. Perceived salience concerns how participants emphasise an issue; analytical importance concerns its explanatory role; policy priority also requires judgement about consequences, equity, feasibility, and local risk. None can be determined by small differences between counts alone. The synthesis proposes relationships among policy functions without claiming statistical causality or independent model validation.

sec.title: 4. Results and discussion
sec.p: The results are organised around nine reported thematic dimensions, followed by discussion of their implications for disaster risk governance, sustainable local development, and local institutional legitimacy. The reported coding-reference counts are presented in the results, with their interpretative limitations explained in Section 3. The findings are thematic summaries of the pooled corpus, without attribution of individual references to actor groups or study sites.

sec.title: 4.1.1 Village regulations and institutions
sec.p: Figure 1 brings together local regulatory availability, village authority, integration of regional rules, standard operating procedures (SOPs) for coordination, policy harmonisation, and guidance. The counts range from 12 to 18 and describe how often these issues were coded. Three observations are relevant to the policy model: rules need to be available and usable; responsibilities need an operational scope; and coordination needs support across government levels. Together, these issues describe the conditions under which village institutions can act.

caption.title: NVivo coding matrix—Village regulations and institutions

sec.p: Local regulatory availability has 18 references, village authority 16, and integration of regional regulations 15. These recurring issues concern the relationship between a formal policy framework and the authority to implement it. A regulation can identify an objective without clarifying the responsibilities, resources, or decisions assigned to village actors. The substantive problem is therefore not simply the number of rules, but whether different levels of government provide compatible responsibilities and practical means of carrying them out. The remaining themes in Figure 1 extend this question to coordination procedures, harmonisation, guidance, and supervision.

A second observation concerns the relationship between authority and support. Village institutions operate within a wider administrative system, so local responsibility cannot be examined independently of the technical and financial assistance available from district/city and provincial actors. Coordination procedures may help make that assistance predictable and clarify how unresolved issues move between levels. The coded material identifies these institutional concerns, but the aggregate chart does not show whether a particular regulation was implemented effectively or whether one site experienced greater uncertainty than another.

C1 connects local mandates with usable guidance and accountable coordination. Clear responsibilities matter because decisions about land use, infrastructure, public services, and preventive expenditure need an institution able to act and answer for its decisions. The effectiveness of these proposed connections remains a question for implementation research.

sec.title: 4.1.2 Disaster risk reduction paradigms, human resource capacity, and disaster literacy
sec.p: Figure 2 categorises volunteer training, community literacy, understanding of DRR, village official capacity, local cadre development, and routine drills. The reported figures range from 12 to 17. These references encompass various forms of capability: residents’ understanding of risk, volunteers’ operational skills, and the administrative capacity required to sustain preparedness. Overall, these elements illustrate complementary needs in capacity building.

Volunteer training had 17 references, community disaster literacy 16, and understanding of the DRR paradigm 15. Together, these themes distinguish skills for organised action from residents’ ability to understand and respond to risk information. The relevant observation is that the reported capacity needs include both individual learning and the arrangements through which skills are maintained and used.

caption.title: NVivo coding matrix—DRR paradigms, human resource capacity, and disaster literacy

sec.p: A second observation concerns continuity. Village official capacity and local cadre development connect learning with the institutions responsible for plans, information, and coordination. The policy implication is that capacity development should extend beyond a single training event: responsibilities, opportunities to practise, and access to technical assistance need to remain available between emergencies. This is an interpretation of the reported capacity concerns, not a finding that a particular training format, schedule, or provider was tested. The pooled counts cannot establish how training needs differed among volunteers, officials, or community representatives.

The third observation links capacity to sustainable local development. Disaster literacy can support the use of risk information in ordinary decisions about settlements, livelihoods, and public facilities, while administrative capability can connect that information with planning and expenditure. Inclusive learning also requires attention to how messages and exercises are made accessible to residents with differing abilities and access to information. The study did not measure changes in knowledge, behaviour, or training outcomes. C2 therefore specifies a policy function—sustaining the capability for preventive and adaptive action—whose delivery and effects require evaluation. It complements the operational facilities in C3 and the production and use of risk knowledge in C7.

sec.title: 4.1.3 Infrastructure, information systems, and preparedness facilities
sec.p: Figure 3 identifies risk maps, evacuation routes and assembly points, vulnerable population data, emergency communications, basic equipment, and early warning systems. The counts range from 13 to 18. The substantive pattern concerns the connection between usable information, physical access, and the facilities needed to act during disruption. These elements describe complementary aspects of operational preparedness.

caption.title: NVivo coding matrix—Infrastructure, information systems, and preparedness facilities

sec.p: Village risk maps had 18 references, evacuation routes and points 17, and vulnerable population data 16. One observation is that preparedness requires a connection between where hazards may affect residents and how residents can reach safety. A map alone does not establish that a route is accessible, that an assembly point is usable, or that assistance is available to someone who needs it. The reported themes support examining these relationships together. They do not provide a technical assessment of facilities or demonstrate that the mapped evacuation arrangements meet the requirements of each hazard.

A second observation concerns the information and communication needed to put arrangements into practice. Population information can help identify assistance needs, while emergency communication and warning systems concern how risk messages reach residents and responsible organisations. Their relationship is operational: information has to be available, understood, and connected with a response procedure. Effective warning also depends on exposure, timing, reach, and response capacity.

The policy interpretation is to treat preparedness facilities as a maintained system rather than a collection of equipment. Responsibilities for the use, maintenance, and review of maps, routes, communication options, and basic facilities need to be assigned. From a sustainability perspective, these arrangements are relevant to protection of life and continuity of essential services, including for residents with mobility or communication barriers. C3 addresses tangible, locally operable infrastructure. C7 separately addresses the production and exchange of risk knowledge. The distinction prevents the model from treating a facility, the information it uses, and the institution operating it as interchangeable. Actual adequacy and maintenance costs require assessment within each locality.

sec.title: 4.1.4 Risk documents and integration into village planning
sec.p: Figure 4 connects disaster management plans, local risk assessments, development-plan integration, contingency plans, operational procedures, and monitoring. Counts range from 12 to 17. The main analytical issue is how risk documents inform decisions rather than whether a document exists. Three observations concern the use of risk knowledge, its connection to routine development planning, and the need to revisit plans as conditions change.

caption.title: NVivo coding matrix—Risk documents and integration into village planning

sec.p: The village disaster management plan incorporates 17 references and 16 local risk assessments, and is integrated into the village’s medium-term development plan and the village government’s annual work plan. These themes connect diagnosis with decisions. A risk assessment identifies concerns that a management plan should address, while development-plan integration provides a route through which those concerns may influence activities and resources. The recurrence of these themes supports examining the relationship, but does not demonstrate that the plans were complete, regularly updated, or used consistently in the six study areas.

Contingency planning and SOPs concern the practical arrangements through which plans can guide action. Monitoring and evaluation concern whether those arrangements remain suitable. These functions address different stages of using and reviewing risk knowledge. The pooled chart does not distinguish a missing document from an existing document that is not used; that distinction is important when deciding what institutional support or technical assistance is needed.

The policy implication is to connect risk assessments, disaster arrangements, and the development planning cycle, including responsibility for implementation and review. This reflects the finding that resilience needs an institutional place in village planning. Sustainability enters through the decisions affected by that integration: the location and design of infrastructure, access to services, land use, and the continuity of livelihoods. A completed planning document is an administrative output, whereas reduced exposure or improved continuity would be an outcome requiring separate evidence. C4 therefore specifies the institutional use of risk knowledge, supported by financing in C5 and data arrangements in C7. The model does not treat the existence of documents as proof that risk-sensitive development has been achieved.

sec.title: 4.1.5 Disaster risk reduction financing
sec.p: Figure 5 groups village budget allocation, regional budget support, mitigation financing, mutual cooperation, budget accountability, and corporate social responsibility (CSR) and partnerships. Counts range from 12 to 17. This pattern identifies public resources, supplementary support, and accountability as related financing concerns. Funding adequacy requires separate expenditure evidence.

Village budget allocation had 17 references, regional budget support 16, and mitigation financing 15. Their recurrence connects local responsibilities with support beyond the village budget. Preventive action, preparedness, and maintenance require resources, while the authority to use those resources depends on the applicable institutional arrangements. The substantive issue is therefore how assigned functions can be sustained over time. The figures contain no monetary amounts or expenditure series and cannot determine whether village allocations were insufficient in the same way across sites or whether regional transfers were predictable.

Mutual cooperation, accountability, and partnerships broaden the financing discussion beyond public allocations. Community contributions may support collective activities, and external partnerships may provide resources or expertise. However, the coding results do not demonstrate the availability, reliability, or distributional effects of these contributions. Unpaid work and household contributions can impose different burdens on residents. Their inclusion in the model therefore requires attention to voluntary participation, transparency, and the continuing responsibilities of public institutions. Social capital should not be assumed to replace public funding.

The policy interpretation is to connect responsibility, resource allocation, and accountability within a continuing planning process. Prevention and maintenance should be considered alongside emergency expenditure, while funding decisions need to be understandable to affected residents. The sustainability concern is whether essential activities can continue without placing disproportionate burdens on poorer households or leaving maintenance unfunded. C5 addresses sustained and accountable financing, including compatible support from different sources. Evaluation would need to examine actual allocations, implementation, maintenance, and who bears the costs. These questions guide future assessment of the model.

sec.title: 4.1.6 Community participation and multi-actor collaboration
sec.p: Figure 6 identifies village deliberation, DRR forums, customary and religious leaders, community volunteers, universities and non-governmental organisations (NGOs), and the private sector. Counts range from 10 to 18. The themes concern where collective decisions take place and which actors may connect knowledge, responsibilities, and resources. Overall, these themes identify potential links between collective decisions and implementation.

Village deliberation had 18 references and village DRR forums 16, followed by customary and religious leadership. These themes identify locally organised spaces through which risk concerns may be discussed and coordinated. Their recurrence does not establish that decisions were inclusive, that participants agreed, or that meeting outcomes were implemented. The analytical issue is whether deliberation has a practical connection to responsible actors and follow-up. Participation becomes relevant to policy design when residents can affect decisions, not simply when a forum or meeting is present.

caption.title: NVivo coding matrix—Community participation and multi-actor collaboration

sec.p: Volunteers, universities, NGOs, and private actors offer different potential contributions to collective action. Their actual involvement, division of responsibilities, duration of partnerships, and flow of resources require source-specific examination. A policy response should therefore clarify roles and accountability before treating the creation of another organisation as the solution.

C6 connects participation with implementation through explicit responsibilities, access to information, and review of agreed actions. Its sustainability contribution concerns whose needs shape development and preparedness decisions and whose interests may otherwise be overlooked. Women, younger residents, people with disabilities, and households with fewer social connections should have accessible opportunities to contribute and challenge decisions. These are design implications rather than measured participation outcomes in this study. The distinction between C6 and C8 is functional: participation concerns the organisation of collective decision-making, while local wisdom and social capital concern cultural and relational resources that may support or constrain it. The presence of customary leaders alone does not establish equitable influence.

sec.title: 4.1.7 Science, technology, and risk data integration
sec.p: Figure 7 groups data-driven warning, agency data integration, digitisation of risk information, geographic information systems (GIS) and participatory mapping, citizen information applications, and technology training. Counts range from 11 to 17. The pattern concerns the production, exchange, interpretation, and use of risk knowledge. It complements the operational facilities in Figure 3 without establishing that a particular technology is effective or suitable for every village.

caption.title: NVivo coding matrix—Science, technology, and risk data integration

sec.p: Data-driven warning had 17 references, agency data integration 16, and risk information digitisation 15. These recurring themes connect technical information with institutions responsible for local action. A dataset can support planning or warning only if it reaches the appropriate actors in a usable form and is linked to assigned responsibilities. The theme concerns integration of official risk information with local use; the chart does not measure interoperability, data quality, warning accuracy, or the timeliness of communication.

GIS, participatory mapping, citizen information applications, and technology training raise a second issue: information systems need users who can interpret and maintain them. Digital availability alone does not establish that residents can access a message or understand what action to take. The policy interpretation is to connect technical support with local capacities and communication practices. Connectivity constraints and the possibility of power or communication interruptions also make it necessary to consider locally usable alternatives. These requirements are implications for design, not comparative findings about particular technologies or documented outage performance.

C7 therefore addresses usable knowledge rather than equipment acquisition alone. It links scientific information and local observations with planning, communication, and review, while keeping responsibility for updating and interpreting information explicit. Its sustainability contribution lies in supporting informed decisions about settlements, infrastructure, services, and livelihoods. The same data may serve several purposes, but local conditions determine what level of detail, access, and support is needed. The study does not establish that digitisation itself produces resilience. Practical evaluation should examine whether information changes decisions, reaches relevant residents, and remains available when required.

sec.title: 4.1.8 Local wisdom and village social capital
sec.p: Figure 8 identifies mutual cooperation, deliberation and consensus, customary religious philosophy, customary elders, religious institutions, and knowledge of natural signs. Counts range from 12 to 18. These themes concern distinct resources: collective practices, decision procedures, authority relationships, and environmental knowledge. Grouping them under local wisdom does not make them equivalent or establish that their influence is uniformly beneficial.

caption.title: NVivo coding matrix—Local wisdom and village social capital

sec.p: Mutual cooperation had 18 references, deliberation and consensus 17, and the customary religious philosophy 16. In the Minangkabau context, local philosophy expresses the relationship between customary norms, Islamic principles, and the Quran. These practices and ideas may make risk communication and collective action locally meaningful. They should not be attributed uniformly to all residents or to culturally distinct settings such as the Mentawai Islands.

References to customary elders and religious leadership concern socially recognised relationships through which information and assistance may circulate. Recognition is not necessarily equal across residents: customary and religious authority may be contested, and opportunities to speak can differ by gender, generation, disability, or social position. The reported themes provide a reason to examine these relationships; they do not demonstrate specific exclusion in the sampled communities. Policy design should retain the potential for mobilisation while asking who can influence decisions and how disagreement is handled.

Knowledge of natural signs raises a related question about how local observations connect with scientific information. Such knowledge may support awareness and locally intelligible communication, but the study did not test its predictive reliability. C8 therefore recognises local wisdom and social capital as conditional resources. Their contribution depends on their relevance to the hazard setting, compatibility with technical warning, and use through inclusive and accountable institutions. This interpretation retains the emphasis on legitimacy and mobilisation while avoiding the assumption that tradition guarantees resilience. The sustainability objective is not simply to preserve a practice, but to examine how it supports the safety, participation, and well-being of different residents over time.

sec.title: 4.1.9 Sustainable development and village resilience
sec.p: Figure 9 connects village social resilience, safe spaces and spatial planning, protection of vulnerable groups, disaster education, environmental and watershed management, and local economic strengthening. Counts range from 14 to 18. The themes identify social, spatial, environmental, and livelihood concerns through which disaster governance intersects with sustainable development. They describe areas of concern rather than measured changes in resilience or development performance.

caption.title: NVivo coding matrix—Sustainable development and village resilience

sec.p: Village social resilience had 18 references, safe spaces and spatial planning 17, and protection of vulnerable groups 16. The substantive observation is that resilience concerns the conditions under which everyday life can continue safely. Decisions about settlements and infrastructure can influence exposure, while protection arrangements need to recognise that residents have different capacities to prepare, evacuate, and recover. These links justify examining risk within development decisions. They do not establish that the proposed governance model has reduced vulnerability or that one social group benefited more than another.

Disaster education and environmental or watershed management each had 15 references, while local economic strengthening had 14. These concerns link the continuity of learning, environmental functions, and livelihoods under recurrent hazards. Priorities should reflect local exposure, consequences, available capacity, and affected residents’ needs.

C9 makes sustainable development and village resilience explicit as the intended outcome orientation of the model. Sustainability also informs the other components: regulations allocate responsibility for risk-sensitive decisions; capacity and facilities support safe action; planning and financing connect risk concerns with investment; and knowledge, participation, and local legitimacy shape how decisions are made. This relationship avoids treating sustainability as an additional programme introduced only after preparedness has been addressed. C9 connects spatial planning, education, social protection, environmental management, and the economy. Evaluating these pathways would require indicators and evidence of changes in service continuity, exposure, livelihood conditions, environmental functions, and inclusion over time. These outcomes were not measured in this study.

sec.title: 4.1.10 Contextual interpretation across study settings
sec.p: This section interprets the hazard and geographical contexts of the six study settings; it does not present a site-by-site comparison of qualitative evidence. Coastal Padang and Pesisir Selatan connect earthquake, tsunami, and flood exposure with warning, evacuation, and continuity of access. The earthquake, slope, and hydrometeorological settings of Padang Pariaman and Agam make the relationship between land use, infrastructure, and preparedness relevant. Tanah Datar’s volcanic and lahar setting connects settlement and river-corridor decisions with warning and evacuation. The Mentawai Islands raise questions about locally operable preparedness, communication, and access between islands. These contexts overlap; they are not mutually exclusive hazard categories.

These contextual contrasts suggest why implementation may need local adaptation. Because the available coding outputs are pooled, differences in thematic emphasis across sites cannot be established. Such comparisons require coded extracts linked to sites, explicit participant coverage, and examination of convergent and contrasting accounts. The present model therefore specifies shared policy functions while leaving their local weighting and configuration open to comparative investigation.

sec.title: 4.1.11 Cross-cluster analysis of key governance relationships
sec.p: Table 6 summarises the analytical interpretation of four governance clusters linking C1, C5, C6/C8, and C3/C4/C7.

caption.title: Analytical interpretation of key governance clusters

td.p: Local responsibilities require clear authority, practical guidance, and procedures for support across government levels.
Financing should cover preparedness and maintenance as well as emergency response, with transparent responsibilities for continuity.
Locally legitimate participation and social capital
Deliberation and mutual assistance may support preventive planning when participation is inclusive and decisions are accountable.
Usable risk information and institutional connectivity
Maps and warnings become useful when information is understandable, reaches responsible actors, and informs planning and response.

sec.p: These interpretations connect authority and financing with the capacity to act, participation and local legitimacy with collective decisions, and usable risk information with preparedness and development planning. The model’s proposed relationships and effectiveness require implementation testing and outcome evaluation.

sec.title: 4.2.1 Authority instruments and operational support
sec.p: The nine coding matrices show constraints that extend beyond a shortage of resources or training. Within disaster risk governance, the public policy perspective helps interpret how problems are recognised, translated into instruments, and connected to organisational responsibilities. Comparative policy research offers useful concepts concerning national policy styles and the governance of emerging technologies, although these studies do not provide empirical evidence about West Sumatran villages (Ruvalcaba-Gomez & Garcia-Benitez, 2026; Tosun & Howlett, 2022). Themes concerning local regulations, village authority, policy integration, and coordination procedures raise a common question: how can provincial, district/city, and village responsibilities become operationally connected? Work on cross-sectoral coordination, policy integration, and environmental policy instruments helps explain this problem (Behnke & Hegele, 2024; Cejudo & Trein, 2023; Head, 2025). These studies concern different policy settings and are used as supporting perspectives, not as proof that the proposed model will work. The interpretation rests on the relationship between reported constraints, rather than the numerical ranking of codes. Unclear mandates can leave actors uncertain about their roles, while incomplete instruments can make implementation dependent on personal initiative. Villages may consequently be expected to implement programmes without corresponding authority or support. The proposed shift is to recognise village institutions as participants in policy decisions, with clear responsibilities, operational guidance, and channels for obtaining assistance. This is an argument for enabling local action within public accountability, not a claim that greater local autonomy is sufficient in every setting. Sustainable development gives this institutional question a practical purpose: decisions about settlements, infrastructure, services, and livelihoods need risk information and accountable responsibility before losses occur.

Recurring themes concerning planning documents, disaster management plans, and integration into village development plans can also be interpreted through policy theory. They indicate a need to shift disaster issues from a sectoral agenda to a development agenda. Theoretically, a policy is strengthened when it is incorporated into regulations and linked to planning, budgeting, and evaluation processes (Cejudo & Trein, 2023; Kim, 2026). The findings therefore show that risk documentation and its integration into planning serve more than an administrative purpose. They provide a mechanism for translating policy declarations into action. From this policy perspective, this integration embeds risk reduction in day-to-day development decisions.

This supporting policy perspective identifies four functions within the governance arrangements. These are recognition of the local risk problem; development of instruments such as regulations, standards, SOPs, and plans; allocation of roles among local government, the Regional Disaster Management Agency (RDMA), village institutions, DRR forums, and other actors; and arrangements for evaluation and learning. These are cross-cutting functions within the nine-component model, not an alternative four-component model. Their analytical value is to show how a list of reported problems can inform policy design without equating recurrent codes with validated interventions.

sec.title: 4.2.2 Disaster management as an operational cycle
sec.p: The capacity, preparedness, and planning themes support examining disaster management as a continuing cycle rather than an episodic response. Volunteer training, disaster literacy, risk maps, evacuation arrangements, management plans, and local risk assessments concern capabilities used before an event, while also shaping response and recovery. Their recurrence identifies preparedness as a relevant governance concern, but does not establish that participants ranked it above every other phase. The disaster management cycle is therefore used as an operational perspective within the model, connecting preventive action with response and subsequent learning.

Research on Hurricane Katrina and public support before and after Hurricane Dorian illustrates the importance of examining disaster policy across time rather than only during an emergency (Comfort et al., 2010; Levitt & Olson, 2025). In the present material, references to maps, vulnerable population data, contingency documents, exercises, and operational procedures concern the capabilities needed to act when an event occurs. This supports an interpretation of preparedness as an organised system involving personnel, information, communication, evacuation options, and learning arrangements (De Sisto et al., 2026; Kusumastuti et al., 2022). Emergency communication, basic equipment, and monitoring also connect preparedness with response and recovery. The relationship between disaster risk science and broader risk science helps place these functions within an ongoing process of understanding and managing uncertainty (Aven, 2025). Their connection is analytical: risk assessment can inform response planning, and post-event evaluation can identify changes needed in prevention. The proposed model makes these relationships explicit so that implementation can subsequently be examined.

The implication for policy models is that disaster-resilient villages should not be reduced to mere volunteer forums or training sessions. The proposed model treats them as village-based disaster management systems that integrate risk recognition, capacity building, operational preparedness, coordinated response, and post-disaster learning. In the multi-hazard context of West Sumatra, understanding this cycle is crucial because geological, hydrometeorological, and social threats can demand different capacities but still require the same policy framework.

sec.title: 4.2.3 Village-based risk governance
sec.p: Findings on participation, regulation, and risk information suggest that village resilience depends on relationships beyond the village’s internal capacity. Risk governance scholarship examines cross-sectoral and cross-level coordination, systemic interdependence, and uncertainty (Hansen & Antonsen, 2024; Schweizer, 2021; Taebi et al., 2022). Village deliberation, DRR forums, customary and religious leaders, and volunteers recurred in the data, identifying potential arenas and actors for collective action. Their recurrence does not establish the strength or inclusiveness of deliberative capacity. References to agency data integration, local rules, and coordination procedures concern the institutional support through which locally organised action may be connected to the wider governance system.

From a risk governance perspective, the relationships among the village government, NDMA, regional government departments, customary leaders, educational institutions, civil society, and the private sector must be understood as an ecosystem. Weaknesses in any one area may impede the wider system. For example, a village may have an active deliberative process. However, its outcomes may be difficult to translate into action if risk data do not reach local actors or regulations do not support mitigation expenditure. Conversely, a local government may have a robust data system, but without social legitimacy at the village level, risk messages will be difficult to translate into collective action. The analysis connects these aspects without assigning them equal empirical weight. Therefore, this discussion emphasises that village-based risk governance must be understood as the establishment of functional relationships between actors, not simply the formation of new organisational units.

Lower coding-reference counts should not be interpreted as evidence of lower policy relevance. The policy question is whether relevant actors can contribute knowledge and resources through accountable arrangements. Universities, civil society organisations, private actors, and public agencies may provide different forms of support, but their roles should follow local needs and explicit responsibilities rather than a numerical hierarchy of themes.

Thus, the discussion suggests that a disaster-resilient village policy framework should encompass three key requirements. First, roles and coordination channels between actors must be clear. Second, there must be recognition of the village government as the primary node of interaction between formal policies and social practices. Third, there must be a mechanism for exchanging knowledge and resources that keeps the system adaptive. These three requirements form the basis for the policy model design in the following section.

sec.title: 4.2.4 Sustainable development, social vulnerability, and village resilience
sec.p: The ninth coding matrix connects social resilience with safe spaces, protection of vulnerable groups, disaster education, environmental management, and the local economy. These themes place disaster governance within the continuity and quality of development. Research on differentiated exposure, community resilience, and social vulnerability supports examining whose safety, services, and livelihoods are protected (Azhar et al., 2026; Fekete, 2026; Imperiale & Vanclay, 2021). The counts show recurrence of these concerns, not participants’ shared definition of sustainability or measured development effects. Sustainability therefore provides the model’s purpose and is also expressed through an explicit outcome-oriented component against which implementation should be assessed.

Theoretically, sustainable development requires the integration of safety, well-being, and environmental sustainability (Elder, 2025; Fisher et al., 2021). The reported themes make this integration relevant at the village level. Environmental and watershed management, local economic strengthening, and disaster education are not separate sectors but are part of resilience. For example, upstream environmental damage can increase vulnerability to flooding or landslides downstream. A weak local economy makes it difficult for households to adapt and recover, while low levels of disaster education reduce the community’s ability to assess risks. Therefore, this discussion emphasises that the disaster-resilient village policy must be positioned as a risk-based local development policy.

Protection of vulnerable groups is another recurring concern. This reinforces the argument that risks are not evenly distributed. Children, women, the elderly, people with disabilities, and poor households often experience the most severe impacts but have the least capacity to respond and recover. Within a sustainable development framework, policies that are insensitive to differential vulnerability will tend to reproduce inequality. Therefore, the design of the policy model produced in this study must explicitly consider vulnerable groups in planning, data collection, evacuation, social protection, and economic recovery. Ultimately, the sustainability theme extends village resilience beyond preparedness to the ability to maintain safe and dignified lives. Policy outcomes should therefore extend beyond the presence of volunteers or documents. They should be reflected in the quality of the village’s living environment, the ability of local institutions to protect vulnerable residents, and the continuity of the community’s socio-economic functions during and after a disaster.

sec.title: 4.2.5 Local institutional legitimacy and social capital
sec.p: The local wisdom theme identifies mutual cooperation, deliberation, customary philosophy, elders, and religious institutions as potentially relevant resources for collective action. Their recurrence suggests that formal policy encounters pre-existing social relationships and sources of authority. These resources are interpreted through local institutional legitimacy: whether residents recognise decision-making procedures and can participate in them. Critical studies of local wisdom and cultural politics caution against assuming that inherited practices automatically support inclusive development (Corry et al., 2025; Roth & Sedana, 2015). Mutual assistance may help maintain evacuation routes or support residents during disruption; deliberation may connect risk information with collective decisions. Yet customary authority can also coexist with unequal influence, generational differences, or limited opportunities for women and vulnerable groups to disagree. These are conditions that policy design must examine, not exclusionary practices attributed to particular sampled communities without evidence. The model therefore links recognition of local institutions with transparent representation, accessible deliberation, and accountability for decisions.

Policies that resonate with local values may be easier to discuss and translate into collective action, but social acceptance cannot be inferred from coding frequency. Local knowledge also does not replace scientific assessment or formal warning. Accounts of natural signs may contribute to awareness, while their reliability needs contextual checking alongside technical information. The proposed relationship is therefore one of critical integration: locally meaningful communication and observations should inform planning, while public responsibilities and evidence-based warning remain explicit. Practical safeguards include accessible meetings, opportunities for less influential residents to contribute, transparent selection of representatives, and documentation of disagreement. Participation should be assessed through influence over decisions as well as attendance. In this sense, local wisdom may support the social infrastructure of policy when its use remains compatible with inclusion and public accountability.

sec.title: 4.2.6 Design of the nine-component policy model
sec.p: The policy model contains nine interconnected components that correspond one-to-one with the reported thematic dimensions in Figures 1–9. These are C1 local regulations and institutional arrangements; C2 DRR paradigms, human resource capacity, and disaster literacy; C3 infrastructure, information systems, and preparedness facilities; C4 risk documents and integration into village planning; C5 DRR financing; C6 community participation and multi-actor collaboration; C7 science, technology, and risk data integration; C8 local wisdom and village social capital; and C9 sustainable development and village resilience. C1–C8 describe conditions and functions for collective action, while C9 makes intended social, economic, and environmental outcomes explicit. Sustainability also informs the purpose and evaluation of the other eight components. The disaster management cycle, monitoring, evaluation, and learning operate across these components; they do not constitute additional components. The synthesis translates related governance problems into proposed policy responses rather than deriving causal relationships or priorities from the numerical ordering of codes. Regulation needs operational support; capacity development needs resources and continuity; risk information needs a route into planning; and cultural legitimacy requires inclusive procedures. These connections are policy propositions to be tested through implementation.

The village is positioned as the central decision-making arena where these components are connected. This addresses the study’s concern with the institutional role of local units within a wider governance system. It does not imply that every village has identical authority or can provide all technical services independently. Formal rules and resources enable local responsibilities; capacities, preparedness systems, and risk information support action; participation and local wisdom shape how decisions are made and understood; and planning connects these contributions with development choices. Figure 10 shows the proposed relationships and feedback from outcomes to subsequent decisions. Table 5 maps the reported themes to the model, while Table 7 gives the full component names and functions. The shorter labels in Figure 10 and Table 5 refer to the same C1–C9 components.

caption.title: Conceptual relationships among the nine components of the disaster-resilient village policy model

sec.title: 4.2.7 Policy model implementation and learning
sec.p: The proposed implementation process comprises six stages. First, risk diagnosis brings together hazard information, vulnerable groups, actors, local capacity, and existing regulations. Official information, participatory mapping, and local knowledge should inform this diagnosis. Second, regulatory strengthening clarifies mandates, budgeting authority, and operational standards through the instruments appropriate to each governance level. Third, institutional development connects village deliberation, DRR forums, volunteers, RDMA, and other regional government departments through explicit responsibilities. Fourth, integration into planning and financing connects risk assessments, development plans, contingency arrangements, and budget allocations. Fifth, operational preparation combines exercises, warning systems, risk communication, and usable facilities. Sixth, evaluation and learning use monitoring, capacity reviews, and experience from exercises or disasters to revise arrangements as risks and local conditions change.

These six implementation stages describe a proposed, iterative process rather than a sequence evaluated by this study. Application should be adapted to the authority, hazard exposure, social relationships, access conditions, and resources of each locality. Implementation should examine both administrative outputs and development consequences, including maintenance of facilities, accessibility of warning and evacuation, livelihood continuity, and the distribution of costs and benefits. Table 7 summarises the nine model components and their relationship to the reported themes.

Table 7 connects reported themes with proposed policy functions while retaining the same nine-component structure throughout the study. At the conceptual level, it links disaster risk governance, sustainable local development, and local institutional legitimacy. At the practical level, it provides a basis for examining regulations, operational support, and village planning arrangements. Its usefulness must be assessed through piloting and evaluation rather than inferred from the presence of a component in the coding matrix.

caption.title: Synthesis of components of the disaster-resilient village policy model

Clarify mandates, authority, coordination, and accountability.
Local regulations, village authority, integration of regional rules, and coordination SOPs.
C2 DRR paradigms, human resource capacity, and disaster literacy
Sustain knowledge, skills, and capacities for preventive and adaptive action.
Volunteer training, community literacy, DRR understanding, village official capacity, cadres, and exercises.
C3 Infrastructure, information systems, and preparedness facilities
Provide usable arrangements for safety and operational preparedness.
Risk maps, evacuation routes and assembly points, vulnerable population data, communication, equipment, and warning.
C4 Risk documents and integration into village planning
Connect risk knowledge with development decisions and review.
Disaster management plans, assessments, integration with village medium-term development plans and annual work plans, contingency plans, SOPs, and monitoring.
Connect responsibilities with sustained, transparent, and accountable resources.
Village budgets, regional support, mitigation funding, mutual cooperation, accountability, and partnerships.
C6 Community participation and multi-actor collaboration
Organise inclusive decisions and accountable coordination.
Deliberation, DRR forums, customary and religious leaders, volunteers, universities, NGOs, and private actors.
C7 Science, technology, and risk data integration
Produce, exchange, interpret, and use locally accessible risk knowledge.
Data-driven warning, agency integration, digital information, GIS and participatory mapping, applications, and training.
C8 Local wisdom and village social capital
Connect cultural and relational resources with policy, subject to inclusion and accountability.
Mutual cooperation, consensus, local philosophy, customary elders, religious institutions, and knowledge of natural signs.
C9 Sustainable development and village resilience
Specify intended outcomes and criteria for evaluating all components.
Social resilience, safe space, vulnerable groups, education, environmental management, and local economic continuity.

sec.title: 5. Conclusion
sec.p: This study identified interconnected constraints in village disaster governance in West Sumatra, including regulatory uncertainty, limited capacity, inadequate preparedness and risk documentation, fragmented financing, and weak connections among formal institutions, knowledge, and community participation. The analysis organised these reported constraints into nine dimensions that link disaster governance with everyday development decisions. The coding-reference counts describe recurrence in the qualitative corpus; they do not establish causal importance or policy priorities.

The theoretical contribution is a contextual synthesis of disaster risk governance, sustainable local development, and local institutional legitimacy. It positions the village as an arena where formal responsibilities, scientific information, and locally recognised practices can inform collective decisions. C1–C8 specify governance conditions and policy functions, while C9, sustainable development and village resilience, specifies intended outcomes and evaluation criteria for the model. Local wisdom is treated as a potential resource whose contribution depends on inclusion, accountability, and the relationship between customary and formal authority.

Practically, the model proposes connecting mandates, skills, preparedness facilities, risk information, planning, financing, and participatory institutions around locally identified risks. Livelihood continuity, essential services, protection of vulnerable residents, safe development, and environmental functions provide criteria for judging the resulting decisions. The implementation stages and feedback relationships are proposals for testing; the study does not demonstrate that adopting the model has improved resilience or sustainability outcomes.

The study is limited to one Indonesian province and a purposively selected qualitative sample. The pooled coding outputs do not establish balanced representation or differences in thematic emphasis across actor groups and the six sites. Future research should compare the model across coastal, volcanic, riverine, landslide-prone, and small-island settings, with explicit participant coverage and source-linked evidence. Longitudinal or implementation studies should examine whether the proposed relationships operate in practice, how responsibilities and costs are distributed, and whose knowledge and needs shape decisions. Transfer to other settings should depend on institutional and cultural fit and observed performance rather than assumed universal applicability.
